One example of that arose in western Canada a few short years ago. Everyone remembers when we had free access to the United States markets with our cattle, our wheat and our flour, under the Wilson tariff. When the Republican party came into power, however, at one stroke of the pen they destroyed that free access of our raw products to their markets and brought ruin and disaster to the Canadian rancher and stockman. I assert with certainty that any trade treaty which is subject to destruction at the caprice of a commercial enemy is fraught with grave danger to this Dominion. I ask hon. gentlemen to consider that, and I ask if they do not find it so. Can we afford to disregard the call of our domestic markets; can we afford to increase our imports from the United States and decrease our domestic production in order to establish a channel of trade say between Switzerland and Canada? Have hon. gentlemen looked at the figure with respect to little Switzerland, up in the mountains? I was very much amazed when I considered them the other day; I found that from Switzerland alone we imported last year goods amounting to $9,170,000, while we sold that country goods amounting to only $1,310,000. Can we afford to establish a channel of trade with that community? One may say that they run the risk of being shut out by us, but can we afford to establish any great channels of trade and commerce between the countries of the world and our own under treaties that may be destroyed in a single moment by a stroke of a pen, which will result in the dislocation of the whole commercial fabric of the country? That is the whole problem. We on this side of the House, rightly or wrongly, believe that every legislative weapon available to the hands of parliament should be utilized at all times for the preservation of the Canadian market for the Canadian people.
Furthermore, and it is on that point that there is an essential difference between us: My hon. friends opposite are more concerned with foreign trade; we are more concerned about domestic trade. They are concerned about developing channels of trade that take our ships, they say, to the seven seas; we are concerned with bringing people to Canada and giving them work to do in the development of our country and at a proper living standard of wages. These are the problems that concern this country, and on an analysis of the 
budget submitted together with the figures prepared by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) it must be apparent that every effort is being made to send our products to foreign lands and buy products produced by cheaper labour under less decent conditions from other countries in the world. Mr. Speaker, nothing is clearer than what that means to this democracy, nothing is clearer than what it means to this Dominion in the end. How can the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Forlie) invite people to these shores if they cannot find employment? The hon. member for Comox Alberni (Mr. Neill) the other day rose in his place and read from a paper that $3,330 had been spent in twelve days by Vancouver. For what? For food for the starving and unemployed. Why? Because there is no industrial life and there is no work for them to do, and there being no work for them to do the municipality had to expend $3,330 in twelve days, or about $300 a day, in providing food for the unemployed. And what is so in Vancouver is so in other communities, and yet the Minister of Finance talks about busy Canada. About busy Canada! He thinks of busy Canada importing manufactured products made in Switzerland and the United States of America.

May I ask the
hon. gentleman a question?
Certainly.
What would my hon. friend do with our surplus products in Canada while he was filling up the home market?
Sell them.
Where?

And what is more, speaking for myself personally, I would develop the markets that are imposed upon the country by the necessity of those who have to buy, as distinct from those who do it from choice. For those who seek Canada as a market from which to buy by choice are men who buy because they think they will get more favourable terms here than elsewhere, and the moment they do not they will go elsewhere. But I desire, in the future as in the past, to develop those markets with countries that seek our products from necessity, and Great Britain at the moment is one of them. Great Britain has to buy our wheat from necessity. She buys from the Argentine from necessity; she buys from India from necessity. Germany is buying to-day from us from necessity, but the day will come when Germany will have the choice between Russia and

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
Canada and then the market that has been established for our goods will be destroyed with dire results to this country. That is the answer which I make to my hon. friend. I say further that there is such a thing as making haste too quickly. I admit that we are living side by side with the most powerful republic in the world, side by side with a people who are the richest in the world for the moment, and the great influence that they exercise upon our economic and commercial life is apparent to every thinking man. We all know that. But, sir, we have survived. Hostile tariffs we have met, hostile legislation we have met, and we have continued a free people making a name for ourselves among the nations of the world; and when they speak here about our status as a nation,, I should like to think of our economic status as well. I should like to think it is possible-and this is a digression-that the combined wisdom and the genius for statecraft of the eminent men who guide the destinies of the British Empire are equal to the task of bringing about an economic union of the states of the British Empire that will more than compare with the United States of America. Such a policy may be premature at -the moment, but I have had the idea in my mind for generations-
Oh, oh.

Of course not generations, but many years. At any rate I do think that the development of our home market and the building up of this country is a matter that we well may consider to be the work, not of a moment or a day, not of a month or a year, but the work of a generation or two if need be. Why, I remember-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Before the hon. member passes from that subject. I agree with him to a great extent regarding empire trade but how would his present argument harmonize with his previous argument with respect to trade with Australia?

I am pointing out that
the difficulty of our situation in the case of Australia was that there was nothing to trade with, and my hon. friend understood that better than anybody else. He desired to trade with them and they would not have it. That is the position with respect to that matter. When I speak with relation to the empire I realize at once the magnitude of the difficulties that have to be encountered, just as the Prime Minister pointed out the difficulties that had to be met in dealing with our constitutional status. So that with relation to the economic status of this Dominion and other parts of the empire, it is not a matter
that can be solved in a single day, by this legislature or that of any other .part of the empire. It is a matter that can only be solved by the common consent of all the parties affected and that would be brought about by a conference such as I suggested. I remember that the late Lord Long gave the better part of the last years of his life to dealing with that problem. He had gone into the detail of every article that was manufactured or produced in every part of the British Empire, and he had dreamed that there might one day be a self-contained empire between the different units of which there might be preferences and defy hostile foreign tariffs. But it is not a matter that can be realized, as I say, in a single day or in a year. It is a matter which must be considered by men of thought, vision and wisdom from every standpoint. Because, as I have said before, this country may endeavour to make progress too quickly. We have much to learn from the old land, much to learn from Great Britain, much to learn from the early pioneers. They did not make the British Empire in a day, and we cannot make this country a self-contained country in a single hour. I answer my hon. friend's question with respect to Australia in that sense. These matters must be dealt with as a whole and not as an isolated question, and the argument I made was the best argument in the world. Because if the British Empire had a tariff with which to deal with other nations then we could make a self-contained unit of it, and found a United States within the British Empire, even as the United States of America has been founded.
I have endeavoured with respect to trade to point out the real, essential difference between us but I want to go a step further and point out the conditions under which we are now trading. Do hon. gentlemen observe that the trade figures indicate the falling off in our exports? Do they realize that the figures for the last fiscal year showed that our exports had diminished as compared with the preceding year, and the trade figures brought down the day before yesterday by the Minister of Trade and Commerce indicate still further shrinkage in our exports to the world? That, I think, is important, it is signficant. The export trade of the United States has been falling. The export trade of Canada is falling. Why? Because the nations of Europe, the war-battered nations of Europe, are getting back to normal conditions, and as they get back to normal conditions and cultivate their

The Budget-Mr. Bennett

soil, they are going to grow more and more of their food requirements and buy less and less from us, and we all know, whether we like it or not, that they are endeavouring at this moment to do it by every means in their power. Russia is once more coming back as a producing country with respect to grains and cereals. For that reason I view with the greatest apprehension, as a danger very serious in its consequences to this country, the diminution in our export trade. Let us look at the figures for January as submitted by the minister a few minutes ago. Those figures indicate a still further shrinkage in our export trade, and with a still further shrinkage in our export trade taking place as it is with the United States, what must be the result? We find the grand total of the export trade of this country for last January was $84,094,694 as against $84,718,819 in January, 1926. For the ten months ended in January the diminution is not a very large amount, it is true, but it is important. For that period our total export trade diminished from $1,115,416,734 to $1,106,018,792. What happens? If these nations in Europe that are buying our goods and those of other countries, find themselves in a position to supply their food and other requirements by their own efforts, it follows beyond all question that that will be a serious interference with the business of this country, and to the extent to which that trade is diminished, to that extent does it work a hardship upon the Canadian people. That hardship can be overcome only by the means which I have suggested, and I know of no other. None other has been suggested. That is the position with respect to the matter.
The minister next dealt with the question of reductions in taxation and I compliment him upon endeavouring to reduce taxation. A 10 per cent reduction in the income tax will undoubtedly effect some benefit, but I ask him whether the 10 per cent is applicable to the total tax the individual pays on the total schedule, or whether each percentage is to be reduced by 10 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The total.

Then the benefit will not be as great as it would otherwise be, because the schedule varies with the extent of the income. A 10 per cent reduction on the different percentages would effect a greater benefit than a 10 per cent reduction on the total.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My understanding is that when the statement is made out, the amount of the tax is calculated and then 10 per cent is taken off.

I am sure that that will
bring some measure of satisfaction to all the people of this country. I hope the income tax will be entirely abolished for reasons which I will presently give.
No.

I understand, because I
have seen the resolutions of bodies of agriculturists in western Canada, and I propose to refer to those resolutions later, but for the moment I desire to congratulate the government on having made this reduction in the income tax.
With respect to the sales tax I can only point out that it has been a very difficult tax to administer, in the sense that it requires expert assistance and help for the purpose of determining in many instances what the tax should be. For example, I think nothing could be worse than to have goods brought in from England with a case containing them, upon which a duty is imposed, and then to have sales tax added to the value of the goods and case and the duty computed upon the total of the sales tax and the value of the goods and case. It .smot sound to tax a tax, and under the present tariff regulations the sales tax is added to the cost of the article and the duty computed upon the sales tax and that cost. That is the present position. It would be in the interest of trade and the development of commerce that that should be removed if at all possible.
I regret t'he minister has not seen fit to afford any relief to those people who desire to make large contributions to deserving charitable objects. Mr. Gladstone in one of his great budgets discussed the question of freeing the income of charities from income tax, but that is not the situation here. In this new country where hospitals have to depend largely upon benefactions obtained from well-minded people, where, in cities like Montreal or Toronto, they maintain efficient hospitals, not at the expense of the public, but by reason of contributions made by their public-spirited citizens, this government might have well considered the idea of freeing from income tax contributions made for that purpose. I had hoped that the minister would do so, because after all the hospital deals with the poor, with the indigent, with the man unable to care for himself, and as regards these facilities that are now seeking millions of dollars in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and other places, how are men going to make contributions if it costs $3,000 to give $10,000? That position is one of great seriousness, and while it may be too late now, I had hoped

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
the minister would give it his favourable consideration. It is important in this country that men of wealth be philanthropic, but how can they be philanthropic if to give away $100,000 it costs them $35,000 or $40,000? The minister might have placed restrictions upon it, made it subject to his approval, or the approval of the government.
The same in the case with respect to education. There are men taking their place in this House to-day who have been able to get their education through the benefaction of one of the greatest and most illustrious statesmen of his age. What would have happened if his benefactions had been subject to an enormous imposition of income tax in South Africa? The subject is one of such a serious character that it might well have been given favourable consideration by the minister.
I leave that; but I now desire to proceed to a discussion of the general problem of taxation as I see it, because it is of the utmost importance that we should arrive at a clear understanding of the matter. This is only my personal view. Had I been differently situated I should have endeavoured to induce my colleagues to consider favourably the views which I now present to the House. The problem of taxation has been a difficult one in all ages and among all peoples. In the early days when votes were limited to men who had property, property only was taxed. The franchise was not held by all the people; it was held only by men of large incomes and of large estates. In some instances the landed people only had votes, and they only, you might say, paid taxes, their property paid taxes. But since the Great war there has been a tendency to increase taxation and to select everything possible for the purpose of imposing taxation upon it. No longer are we taxing thrift as we used to do; we are taxing what is to be. We are taxing turn-over and sales; we are imposing taxes upon business which we expect to come to us.
More than a century ago Adam Smith laid down certain principles with respect to taxation. At that time the franchise was held by a limited number of people. It is now held by all men of twenty-one years of age and women too of that age in Canada and the United States, and therefore the four principles he laid down are no longer entirely applicable to our condition, but they must be added to. He laid down four principles:
1.	Equality of taxation.
2.	Certainty of taxation.
3.	Convenience of taxation.
4.	Economy of taxation.
Those are the four principles which Adam Smith declared should be considered by all
32649-26J
tax-levying bodies. But it seems to me that the time has come when a new principle must be added. I have followed with some interest in the days that are past the arguments advanced by leading tax experts in this country with respect to this matter, and I think the suggestion that has been made that universality is another principle to be applied, is a correct and proper one. In other words, if every man or woman has a right to vote in this country, we should if possible provide, as they did in the days of Adam Smith, that every person who votes to determine what form of government we shall have should also pay some tax. I do not care how little it is, they should make some contribution to the maintenance of our country's institutions.

Do I understand
that the hon. gentleman is suggesting that everyone over twenty-one years of age under our present system of taxation does not pay a tax?

I am coming to that in
just one moment. If my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) will hear the rest of it, he will realize what I have in mind. Not only should they be taxed, but, if possible, it should be a visible tax. The next principle is visibility. Universality and visibility.
Are there any hon. members in this House who do not realize that there are thousands of their constituents who have no realization of the taxation problem. How many men and women realize that they are paying taxes? How many elections have been run in this country on the question of taxation pure and simple? It is true that in England that is the case, but how many times in this country have the electors been asked to deal with the problem of taxation pure and simple? If you have a tax that is felt .and known as a tax by every man and woman over twenty-one, a tax .that is universal in its application, I am certain that it would do much to improve conditions in this democracy, and to improve the conditions under which we labour.
My idea is this. It is not original at all. You may have seen it presented by the late Sir Edmund Walker in addresses he made to the shareholders of his bank from time to time. He believed in a universal turn-over tax, a tax by which every man who buys something will be able to make some contribution, a known contribution, a percentage levy. It is simple, it is universal, it is convenient, it is equal, it is easily collected -it has all the qualifications that were mentioned by the late Adam Smith, and in
The Budget-Mr. Bennett

addition to that it meets with modern conditions, and will help solve many of the difficulties that we have in this country today. Until men and women have a realization of the money that the state is spending, and where the money comes from, there will not be that intelligent appreciation of the difficulties and responsibilities of government that is so essential for the maintenance of this Dominion, and I do suggest that the Minister of Finance would be well advised to consider whether or not-there is still time- he could not devise some tax along those lines that would not have the objectionable features that attach to the so-called nuisance taxes or to the sales tax as such. As between the sales tax and a tax upon turn-over, which includes a tax upon everything that men buy, you would be able to get revenue more readily by a turn-over tax, and in larger quantities, and you would be able to make a decrease in the income tax without any difficulty in the world, because it is all a mistake, I say to my friends from the west, to think for a single moment when politicians go about the country and tell the people that taxation is all imposed on the rich man and none on the poor, that such is the case. It is not so. Every man makes a contribution to the state; everyone knows that is so. But if we impose a tax based upon the expenditures of the people, then, as the poor man has less to spend than the rich man, his contribution will be correspondingly less, but because he exercises the franchise he will make some contribution to the life of the state in the form of taxation.
I do say that it is a wholly erroneous proposition to say to the people of this country that the poor man should pay no taxes, and then say that he should vote. No man should vote who does not pay taxes, and every man who votes should pay taxes, and, as a corollary, every man who pays taxes should vote. I make that suggestion to my hon. friend, because it seems to me that this sixtieth anniversary of our confederation might be a reasonable time to consider the whole problem of taxation. Sir Edmund Walker urged it on the people of this country until he grew weary of so doing. We were more concerned ini taxing people by methods and means that they could not see, than in providing taxation that they could see and understand, and to the extent to which the people are self-deceived in this matter, it is injurious to the country. I am certain of that. While it might seem to work a hard-

ship with respect to some individuals, I am sure that in the end it would be found attractive, and would solve many of the difficulties that now confront us.

Would the hon.
gentleman suggest that the extent of such a tax as he proposes would be visible?

I am sure my friend from Winnipeg North Centre will realize the soundness of the observation of the late Mr. Gladstone-"I cannot prescribe till I am called in." That is the only answer that I can make. I cannot say to what extent it would be made, because that would depend upon the necessities of the occasion. The revenue requirements of the country, with expenditures cut down to the limit, would determine what percentage of turn-over taxation should be imposed.
Let me proceed to the other question, one that is wrapped up in this whole problem, the question of our national debt. I wonder if the Minister of Finance could not devise a better means than he has suggested of dealing with this problem. I am going to offer to the House a suggestion as to the solution of the problem of our national debt, and I will ask the Minister of Finance to give it his most careful, I cannot say necessarily favourable, consideration.
We have in this country coming due this year, in 1927, a total debt of $100,505,650. Here let me say that the observations made by the Minister of Finance with respect to reduction in the national debt are hardly correct statements. They have been made by successive ministers of finance; they are found in the official gazette, but the truth is that the deadweight debt of this country was reduced last year by $43,000,000. The deadweight debt was reduced to the extent of $8,000,000 in treasury notes, and $35,000,000 of bonds, which were retired out of surplus earnings of the country-a total of $43,000,000. That $43,000,000 was a reduction in the deadweight debt of the country, but in the report that appears in the Canada Gazette, and in the statements made from time to time, we have reduction in debt, and increase in debt, that takes into account not only the deadweight debt of the country, but also the bank balances and the adjustments that take place from time to time in the department. Except as to the retirement of the $43,000,000, there has been no reduction in the deadweight debt of the country, because none of it came due, and the department has purchased none of the debentures or bonds in anticipation of their maturity. So I think it might be desirable

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
in the future to show in the Canada Gazette the changes in the deadweight debt of the country. Every chancellor of the exchequer in England differentiates between deadweight debt and other obligations, and if we placed in the Canada Gazette a statement showing that the deadweight debt is the same to-day as it was on the 1st of January, that would be a correct statement because the deadweight debt has been reduced only by the retirement of $35,000,000 of bonds on November 1st, and a further $8,000,000 of treasury notes, making a total of $43,000,000.
I have an observation to offer to the House. I have given this matter considerable attention, but perhaps my solution will not commend itself at all to the House. We have $100,000,000 coming due this year. How are you going to meet that? Some we will pay out of surplus. How is the rest to be paid, and what rate of interest are the new obligations to carry? I propose, first, that the Minister of Finance should submit to parliament a bill to create a consolidated four per cent security of the Dominion of Canada, and I propose that the Canadian people should pay off that debt without being conscious of so doing.
What about visibility?

It is going to be very
visible to the people who pay it, but the Canadian people themselves at the moment will not have to pay it. The visibility will come in, in a moment. First, has this House considered who are the great custodians of the wealth of this country? There are two great custodians-the chartered banks and the life insurance companies. The chartered banks to-day have money assets of approximately $2,900,000,000. The insurance companies doing business in Canada are custodians of assets of the Canadian people to the extent of $1,250,000,000. Do you realize, Sir, that the Canadian people have outstanding at this moment insurance on their lives aggregating $5,000,000,000? Do you realize that the revenue derived from the insurance on the lives of Canadians in Canadian companies will this year amount roughly to $215,000,000, and that the income of British and foreign companies operating in this country will amount approximately to $70,000,000; that the disbursements to be made by the Canadian companies will amount roughly to $130,000,000 and by the other companies, British and foreign, to approximately $40,000,000? So that this year we may say that the surplus money derived by the insurance companies from premiums upon the lives of Canadian citizens will amount to over $110,000,000. Those insurance companies really hold this money as trustees for their policyholders, because the law imposes upon the insurance companies the obligations of management and investment under such conditions as will ensure the return of between three and three and a half per cent.
Therefore I propose that the Minister of Finance should, after creating bis four cent consolidated Canadian securities, provide by legislation that a percentage, to be hereafter determined, of the revenue of the insurance companies, amounting to a net total of over $110,000,000 this year, and from the deposits of the Canadian people in our savings banks, amounting approximately to at least another billion and three quarters, should be utilized for the purpose of paying off this $100,000,000. This four per cent security I would maintain at all times at par-a very simple process. Under our Finanoe Act, our Department of Finance operates practically as a federal reserve board and all that the insurance companies would have to do if they required additional money would be to deposit, either through their banks or with the Minister of Finance, the four per cent consolidated securities and receive the money from the federal reserve board. All that the banks would have to do would be what they have already been doing, as you will observe from the returns brought down by the Minister of Finance, deposit these securities with the Minister of Finance and obtain for them the money which enables them to carry on their business.
Now, Sir, if we adopted some such plan as this by which the savings of the people would be made available to take care of the obligations that mature this year, we will have done two things; first of all, we will have provided for those who have policies-of insurance an unquestioned and stable security; secondly, we will have enabled the banks, who pay three per cent on their deposits, by purchasing a small quantity more in addition to the securities they now hold to add a measure of stability to their own assets. In addition to all that we will have provided that the interest upon that part of our loan which is not met out of surplus will be paid to Canadian people and not to foreigners. That I consider to be a matter of vast importance at this time. Lastly, we will have saved, not a million dollars as my hon. friend the Minister of Finance asserts, but by adopting such a plan we will have saved for the people of this country next year and the years following not less than $1,700,000.
The Budget-Mr. Bennett

I submit, Sir, that the time has come, for this parliament in the exercise of its unquestioned authority and power, to say that these deposits of the people should be utilized to the extent necessary to provide for the maturing obligations not met out of surplus. At the same time we would have created a security that would rank with the consols of England, a consolidated four per cent Canadian security that could be issued from time to time. Mark you, we have over a billion dollars of the national debt maturing before the end of 1937. If we took care of these maturing obligations in the manner I have suggested we would save to the Canadian people 815,000,000 per annum, which saving if utilized as an amortization fund would, within the period that England has fixed for the payment of her debt to the United States, retire the national debt of this country and leave us a country free of obligations.
Now, mark you, Mr. Speaker, I submit this not as embodying the views of my colleagues behind me, but merely as representing the views that I have arrived at after giving the matter some consideration and attention over a period of years, believing that if I had an opportunity I might be able to convince my colleagues of the soundness of such a measure, which, properly worked out, would assure, as I have said, stability to the savings of the people of this country, placing their security upon an unquestioned level of safety, and at the same time giving to the people the opportunity of having their resources utilized in reducing our national obligations incurred by reason of the war and its after effects.

Would my hon. friend
permit a question before he leaves that subject? The percentage figure would, I take it, be rather vital in any such scheme. He has given a great deal of thought to the question, and I should like to have his view as to what percentage it would be necessary to levy.
That is the turnover tax?

No, this security. My
hon. friend mentioned a percentage.

My hon. friend the Minister of Railways has asked a very pertinent question. I say the life insurance companies have to make deposits, and those deposits are increased from year to year by reason of the increased business they transact, as my hon. 'friend knows. There is in force in Canada at the moment life insurance of not less than 85,000,000,000, and the assets of the life insurance companies amount to not less than a billion and a quarter dollars, and the surplus

premiums available for investment by the life insurance companies during the year amount to not less than 8110,000,000. The banks have not less than a billion and three-quarter dollars saving deposits, probably more, and if you take the loan companies and the provincial savings banks the total deposits probably amount to at least 82,000,000,000. Now, the only problem is the problem of an adjustment. I propose that each of the insurance companies and each of the banks should make up the balance of the hundred million dollars to be provided for this year after taking into account the surplus which I understand the Minister of Finance hopes will amount to about twenty million dollars. That would leave $75,000,000 to 880,000,000 to be distributed between the banks and insurance companies in consolidated four per cent securities. The banks and the insurance companies would suffer no loss, except a possible interestearning power, because my friend the Minister of Railways must have observed from the last return of the Finance department with respect to the banks the vast unemployed sums of savings that they have in their hands. These would be available for that purpose. I would not deprive the banks of their earning power because they are paying three per cent on their deposits and would be getting four from this security. If they require more money to maintain the equilibrium between demand loans and demand deposits and between time loans and time deposits the federal reserve board-the Finance department-would provide for their requirements. It would be a continually revolving credit scheme. That is the conclusion at which I have arrived.

Does the scheme
involve setting up something of the nature of a federal reserve bank?

No, Mr. Speaker, because we already have it-the Finance department to-day is a federal reserve bank. I suppose my friend studies the bank returns in the Canada Gazette. If so, he will have observed that the banks from time to time are borrowing from the Finance department sums of money on deposit of bonds of the Dominion of Canada and other securities.
Under the Finance Act.

Yes. That information
was contained in an answer by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to a question asked the other day by the hon. member for We-taskiwin (Mr. Irvine).

The Budget-Mr. Bennett

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I wonder if I understood my
hon. friend clearly. Under his plan would we pass legislation to compel insurance companies to loan a certain amount of money at four per cent?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And if so, to that extent would it not reduce the profits to the policy holders?

I have endeavoured to
point out that the object is not to compel the lending of money but to do in amplified form what we have now done, to make it compulsory that part of their investments shall be made in four per cent consolidated bonds of Canada. Undoubtedly, to the extent to which they utilized these four per cent securities, there would be a diminution in the interest rate, because the average rate earned by Canadian companies to-day is roughly over six per cent while that earned by American companies is approximately over five per cent. But we should select the form of investment.
I did not bring into the chamber with me from my room the insurance returns, but if hon. gentlemen are interested enough to examine the investments of the insurance companies they will find that they have a large number of just such securities-guaranteed Canadian Northern, guaranteed Grand Trunk Pacific, and some of our own securities. If we deal with the matter in the manner I have indicated it would only be doing what we did during the war; it would compel them to make investments of certain kinds. The government has already proposed in this session to increase the deposits made by these insurance companies. If my suggestion were carried out there would be some diminution in interest profits, but in view of the fact that there are such vast profits earned over and above the money necessary to take rare of reserves at three and three and a half per cent, no hardship would be imposed upon the Canadian people, who would realize that their savings, although the profits of the life insurance companies might be affected-and as my hon. friend knows, life insurance is intended for protection rather than for profit-would be available for the whole of the people, while the trusteeship obligation imposed on the companies would be better discharged by reason of the stability and certainty of the securities.

Many of these insurance
companies are also large mortgage loan companies. If I rightly understand the hon. member's suggestion, it would open up another field of investment. Would that not leave a shortage of money for business in other directions?

It would work no hardship on anyone with respect to this year, because we have only $100,000,000 coming due this year. Does my hon. friend realize that it coat us $3,000,000 for the flotation of loans last year? That amounts to three per cent on $100,000,000.

Merely for purposes of
clarification, and summarizing my hon. friend's scheme, is it not really compelling the insurance companies and the banks to loan money to the government at four per cent regardless of the current rate?

My hon. friend has not
correctly stated it.

I just want to have it
put correctly; I am not indulging in any captious criticism. -

By putting a question
you think you expose a fallacy. I know you well enough.
Louder.
I was making an observation to the Minister of Railways which he quite understood; it was not necessary for the rest of the House to hear.
Oh, oh.

It is not compelling the banks nor the life insurance companies to lend their money; it is merely providing a trustee security that would prevent the occurrence of another Home Bank failure, for instance, or the breaking up of an insurance company as happened many years ago, because the rate reserved for interest on life insurance investments in this country is fixed by statute at less than four per cent, and it would leave a substantial profit, both to life insurance companies and to the banks, if my proposal were put into effect. I repeat, it is not compelling them to lend, but merely providing a compulsory trustee investment, which is but an amplification of the present provisions of the Life Insurance Act.

But a controlled rate
of interest.

Just as Goschen carried
through his great conversion scheme, and just as two chancellors prior to him were compelled to convert securities in England, so this country in the present moment of stress and strain should utilize the savings of the people in the interests of the whole population.
The Budget-Mr. Bennett

I understood the hon.
member to say that one effect would be to reduce the profits of the companies.
Yes.
Is a further effect not likely to be an increase in the premium charged policy holders?

I am, of course, only
elaborating a plan that has grown in my mind after some consideration, and it does not follow that the plan is at all sound in detail, for I have not worked out the details. ' However, replying to my hon. friend, let me point out that the premium rates now charged, with the present rate of interest reservation as provided by statute, yield an ample surplus which results in large profits; and the effect of the diminution of profits could not possibly work a hardship upon Anybody while it would be to the advantage of the Canadian people. We did it during the war. We imposed that restriction then with respect to deposits of life insurance companies and their investments.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have trespassed a considerable time on the attention of the House, and while I have covered a good deal of ground there are many matters to which, in detail, I shall find it necessary to devote some attention when the resolutions are before us in committee. May I before concluding point out that although there have been fifty-two references to the tariff advisory board there are no recommendations from that board before the House for consideration. A year has gone by and no provision of any kind is forthcoming with respect to the deliberations and the findings of the board. Why was the budget introduced nine days after the reassembling of parliament? I will tell you why, Mr. Speaker. Pressure on the part of those people who are vitally interested in the tariff was so strong that the Minister of Finance had either to yield or to deliver his budget and get away from the agony. He chose to deliver his budget and so obtain some relief, as of course he had a right to do. Now, while budget speeches in days gone by have been delivered early in the session-a reference to the dates will show this-I can recall no session in w'hich the budget has been delivered virtually nine days after parliament has met. And the only reason the minister can have for bringing down his statement so hastily this year must be his desire to escape embarrassment in relation to the tariff advisory board. The board can, of course, take no action; it can but state the facts, and when the facts are made known it is for the minister to act. And the minister, with his high 
regard for Canadian industry, with busy Canada ever in his mind, thought it better to avoid dealing with those complex problems that have been submitted, fifty-two in number, for the consideration of the board, of which references, I learned this morning, thirteen had been disposed of. Returns have been made in respect of thirteen of the fifty-two, but of these we have none before the House now for study. In the absence of any information on the subject we are now told that the tariff continues.
How rests it with the Minister of Immigration? I wonder whether in the dark recesses of his mind he ever reflects upon those halcyon days gone by, when from this side of the House he unburdened his logic and free trade sentiments upon an admiring House? I wonder how my well known protectionist friend, the Minister of Finance, is able now to induce the Minister of Immigration to believe that, after all, all is well in Israel. There are no changes; the status quo must continue. Where then are the tales of that ancient past, that long ago when vituperation and the thun-derings of the Minister of Immigration and some of his friends reverberated through this chamber? What has become of it all? Gone, forgotten, remembered no more. And why? Because the hon. gentleman has been taken into camp and all is well in Israel. At any rate, it does occur to me that we see therein an excellent reason why this budget is being introduced at this early stage. I congratulate the Minister of Finance upon his decision to make no further attacks upon Canadian industry. I congratulate him upon the courage he has shown in retaining the one legislative weapon whereby he may protect the Canadian workman and see to it that he gets something to do. I congratulate him upon his desire to see that Canadians shall be occupied instead of being idle. But I say, Mr. Speaker, that this country must have more people; otherwise it cannot continue to function as a nation. You can only get more people in this country by making it more desirable for men to live in, and you can only make it more desirable to live in by providing work for the men who come to live here. Why do not my hon. friends cheer now?

I did. It is your
method I do not like.

My friends emulate it so often that they must indeed admire it. But in all seriousness let me ask how we can hope to get people into Canada; how does the minister hope to get additional people into Canada?

They are coming.

Diamond Jubilee of Confederation

Yes, and in a consul's
office the other day I saw a list of those who desired to leave; when my hon. friend says they are coming, they are coming to go. We are becoming a community where these people seek an abiding place until they may find a home to our south. That, Sir, we must stop, and we can only stop it by giving employment to our people, and we can only give employment to them if industry is profitable and productive. I fully respect the opinions of others in this matter, but I do know that the reading of those figures during the last two days has convinced me that we are buying millions and millions of dollars worth of goods, in fact hundreds of millions of dollars worth, from foreign countries, giving employment to foreigners and in many instances to Canadians who have left this country when we should be giving employment to our own industrial workers.
I am satisfied that the minister will not be able to keep people in this country unless we make a determined effort to develop our great natural resources rather than export them in the raw state. Rather than do that we must manufacture and fabricate them ourselves and so give employment to our citizens so that they will be able to become Canadians and make their homes here. I know the difficulty of that problem; I have not lived in western Canada for all these years for nothing. I have heard the farmer declare time after time that he has to sell his wheat in the open market and he should buy his goods there. But we must realize now that we must so adjust our commercial and financial system as to meet successfully the competition of the world in our markets, unless we are to become hewers of wood and drawers of water and send our raw material out of this country to give employment to the workmen of other lands.
The fact remains, Sir, that this country has made progress under just such a system, and to the extent that we have interfered with it the country has gone back, as the population shows. The greatest indictment that can ibe brought against the Canadian people and Canadian governments is that we have not been able to retain the people we have brought here, let alone take care of our own natural increase. But in my judgment we have made the greatest contribution to history, in one sense, that the world has ever known. There has never been a people so few in number, inhabiting a country so vast, who have accomplished so much. We have provided facilities by railways and canals for 25,000,000 people; we have envisioned a future of hope and faith, yet the fact remains that the great years of our struggle are now upon us.
The courage, the enterprise, the resourcefulness and fortitude of the Canadian people have made possible this Dominion. For sixty years we have grown in stature, in power and in position in the world, but reading the figures of to-day in the light of world history we must determine one of two things. We must decide whether from choice we will permit our resources to be diverted into foreign channels or whether, with courage and fortitude, we will continue to plough our furrow and go our appointed way, building slowly but surely, knowing-aye, knowing- that the day is not far distant when the very people whose high tariffs and offensive legislation have kept us out of their markets will have to come to us for the raw materials on which to subsist. That is one great vision before the Canadian people,
I congratulate my friend the Minister of Finance to-day; he has yielded to no importunities and to no pressure; he has at least maintained his faith in the fiscal system under which this country has grown great, and on the maintenance of which its future integrity depends.

On section 2-incorporation:

When the motion on which this bill is based was before the House I took some exception to the activities as outlined of this proposed committee, as well ias with its personnel. It seems to me in the first place that this is an excessively large amount for a celebration which, as far as we can determine, will consist very largely of flag-waving, especially when we do not have, as at the present moment, a distinctly Canadian flag to wave. It seems to me that if the people of Canada wish to celebrate a great event such as this, a considerable number of voluntary contributions might be available, and then all the money would not be taken directly out of the pockets of the people. I am quite well aware that in the budget speech a good deal has been said, as usual, about the prosperity of the country, but I also remember that we have at present absolutely no provision for the very considerable number of people unemployed at this particular time in Canada, and whenever fwe introduce a measure calling for social legislation to meet needs of this character we are told that the finances of Canada are not in ia position to stand the strain. I sribmit that as long as there is a single person in need in this country we ought not to go into an extravagant expenditure of this character. We have just passed through the Christmas season, when the most pathetic appeals were made in almost every city of this country by charitable institutions of all kinds for the relief of the poor and the distressed. I take it, Mr. Chairman, that these considerations ought to 'be in our minds before we accede to the suggestion that has been made by the government in regard to this matter.
We read that in the olden days when the Jews wanted to celebrate a jubilee, they allowed the debtors and the slaves to go free. I would suggest that something of that kind might very well mark a celebration of nature. We have an enormous national debt. If we could in some way get rid of a proportion of that debt it would permit of a great deal more rejoicing than we would have under a scheme of this character. In the days of feudalism when there was a great celebration we are informed that they roasted a whole ox and allowed everybody to come to the feast. In this instance we are preparing for very elaborate and somewhat exclusive celebrations. It is something like asking a few people to a turkey dinner who quite habitually dine on chicken. As I read the long list of dignitaries and functionaries, with the exception of the hon. member for Southeast

Grey (Miss Macphail) of course, I notice there are a very large number who occupy official positions, and I submit that the great majority of the people of Canada will have very small opportunity to participate in these festivities. We are inviting outside visitors, accustomed to very frequent celebrations, and will provide very elaborate entertainment for them, but what about the mass of the people across the countiy who will pay the bills? The Prime Minister told 119 the other day that the committee was generally representative. I observe that there is a long list of names, but I am not sure that the committee is representative of the rank and file of the people. The Prime Minister also told us that it would not do .to put any representative of labour, for example, on the committee as that would amount to class representation. I note, however, that the names of the president of the Canadian National railway and the president of the Canadian Pacific railway appear in the list. Mr. E. W. Beatty, the president of the latter organization, said the other day in a pamphlet which was published by the Canadian Pacific Company that the Canadian Pacific was Canada's first citizen. If that statement goes unchallenged -and I had rather thought the Prime Minister himself might be considered Canada's first citizen-and if the Canadian Pacific is Canada's first citizen it is quite fitting that the president should be on this committee. But if the president of a private corporation is to be on this board there is no reason why the president or other officials of leading public organizations should not be there also. If the celebration is to foe truly educational in its character, and I have gathered from the public announcement that such is to be the intention, it is quite fitting that there should be representatives of the organized teachers on the committee. I observe that there is to be a representative of the Canadian Battlefields Memorial Association. Looking to the future of the Canadian people I fancy that the presence on the board of some of the teachers of the country would be of immensely greater importance than that of the president of the Canadian Battlefields Memorial Association. On the committee there are also to be representatives of several women's organizations, among them the Imperial Order of Daughters of the Empire. I have no particular objection to this society being represented, but I would submit that whilst this organization numbers a membership of a few thousand, there are other groups of people in this country who number hundreds of thousands. I think of some of our newer citizens, hundreds of thousands of whom have

Diamond Jubilee of Confederation
located in this country-for example the Ukrainians. Perhaps eastern people hardly realize the extent to which our immigration policy has brought to this country, for good or bad, a large alien population. These people are now located in Canada and playing the part of good citizens. I am glad to note that we have one representative of the Ukrainians sitting in this very corner of the House. He is simply the forerunner of scores of others who will foe here very soon, and other nationalities will have their representatives. What about these people in connection with such a celebration as this? I submit that if it is right to have a representative of the Imperial Order of Daughters of the Empire, we might also, looking to the future unification of the peoples of this country, have a representative from the newer Canadians who are locating in such great numbers in western Canada.
I do not want to labour the matter, but if we are to have a celebration I would urge .that it be made distinctly educational in character, and instead of consisting largely in the glorification of what our forefathers did sixty years ago it might be made a means for binding together the different parts of this Dominion and for remedying some of the weaknesses and evils which exist even under the system of confederation.

I had not the slightest idea that labour had been refused a place on this committee. Nor did I know, until one of the hon. members in this corner mentioned the fact to me, that my name is on the committee. I love Canada. There is nothing odd about that because it is my native land. I have never lived in any other country, and I do not intend to, I would like very much to have Canada happy and merry at this diamond jubilee, but I would also wash it to take stock of itself. If we could have a celebration free from these crazy military parades I should like it very much. The visitors who are coming to us for the celebration should be impressed with the importance of the work we are doing-I do not mean the people here but the people back home; and if the visitors are in a position to learn something of our industries, something about the fine work our people have done, something of our possibilities for the future, I should be very glad indeed to be identified with such a celebration. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Woodsworth) was quite right when he said that we are asking people to a banquet who have too many banquets, whereas those who, possibly, have not even enough food, certainly not enough of beauty or culture or the more delectable things of life, will not
have any part in this celebration. I want to protest against the using of my name without my consent because I am the representative of a class group. I represent agriculture. If I do not, I represent nothing at all, and if I cannot go on the committee as the representative of a class, I will not go on at all, because that is the whole philosophy of my political life. If labour has no place on the committee, then I say agriculture will have no place either, and I ask that my name be withdrawn.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Might I say to my hon. friend (Miss Macphail) that in proposing that her name be inserted as one of the national committee, I did so because she holds a distinguished and historic place in this country as the first woman to be a member of the parliament of Canada, and it is as a member of the parliament of Canada, which represents all classes, all creeds, and all the people of this Dominion, that I hope she will allow her name to remain. I did not ask 'her permission; I have not asked the permission of any one whose name is on this list. I refer to myself because I have a certain special responsibility in presenting the names of the national committee. Some beginning has to be made with the organization of a celebration if there is to be a national one. The government might have taken the matter in hand and dealt with it departmentally. The Department of Trade and Commerce or my own office-that of Prime Minister-might have undertaken, so far as the government was concerned, the carrying out of the celebration. We felt, however, that it would be more in accord with the wishes of the people of Canada generally if the matter were treated, not as a departmental or party matter, but as broadly national in character and we therefore are seeking to have a national committee organized.
As I explained the other night, to get a representative committee of any size organized, some group of individuals have to be brought together to undertake the preliminary work of organization. The government was faced with the alternative of having a committee that would be chosen because of the representative character of the persons who are on it, having regard to what we refer to as an official list, or of seeking to embrace in one committee all the societies and organizations that might wish to have representation on a body of the kind. When one began to go over the lists of the different organizations, one was confronted immediately with a variety of considerations. Education, for example, comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces; if the educational institutions

Diamond Jubilee of Confederation
of one. province were to be put on the provisional committee then we would have to have on the committee representation from the educational organizations of every province.
Why not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Because al!
that kind of representation will be worked out by the executive committee that will have the actual celebration in hand. I am coming to that phase. I am seeking now to explain that the purpose of the government in putting the names it did on the list is simply to form an incorporated' body that will have authority to form an executive, which executive will be charged with the duty of carrying out whatever arrangements may be thought best to make the celebration all that my hon. friends opposite would wish it to be.
Let me come to the next consideration, the matter of religious organizations. I assume that religious organizations will wish to take part in the celebration of the diamond jubilee. If we begin on a provisional committee to include one religious organization, then we shall have to include the others. I have at the moment before me a letter received from the Catholic Women's League of Canada, a very important organization, requesting that the name of the president of that organization should be added. I have no objection; in fact I would like very much to see the name of that lady added to the list. But if her name is added, immediately there will be some Protestant organization that will feel that it should be represented, and the name of its president will have to be included. All denominations will be demanding representation on religious grounds.. If we take the patriotic societies, there are the St. Andrew^ society, the St. Patrick's society, the St. George's society, the St. Jean Baptiste society, and other organizations that will undoubtedly be participating when the week of celebration arrives. If we are to have the heads of all these organizations on a provisional committee to form an executive, one can see in a moment that the numbers will be unwieldy. What the government has done is to take for the personnel of the national committee those whom the citizens of this Dominion themselves have so to speak decided should be, in this particular year, the representative citizens of the Dominion. Their Excellencies the Governor General and Lady Willingdon are here in a representative capacity. The lieutenant governors who are at present in office happen to be the lieutenant governors of this year and their names have been included without regard to who they are or

from what party they may have come. The premiers of the different provinces are included, not because they belong to any particular party or are interested in any political group, but because they happen in this year, 1927, to be the premiers of the different provinces. A certain number of members have been chosen who are privy councillors, in some cases because they are members of the present government; in others because of membership in previous administrations. In two or three cases in particular names have been inserted because they are those of the oldest members of the Canadian parliament. The names are chosen from different political parties so that no one party will be in a position to control the situation. The presidents of the railways have been chosen for the reason that in the matter of preliminary organization probably no advice will be more helpful to a committee than that which can be given by the executives of our great railway organizations. Moreover, we may have occasion during this celebration to expect a good deal of the two great railway systems, and I think the recognition of their presidents on this provisional committee is one that will commend itself pretty generally to the country.
May I make it perfectly clear that there has been no desire to exclude anyone? The idea as regards names has been simply to find a representative group which will comend itself to the country at large because of its representative character as a group that can be entrusted with the duty of selecting an executive. The executive will then begin to discover all of the organizations in Canada that wish to participate in the celebration and will seek to make the celebration what public opinion undoubtedly will expect it to be. There is no question that the educational side of the celebration will be the first and main feature of it, and that every effort will be made by the executive committee to link up every Canadian organization that should be included. But that is a task which an executive committee is much better able to carry out than a very large committee. I repeat that it would be extremely difficult to suggest any committee from which a very large number of most appropriate names would not be excluded. I wish to emphasize to the committee the fact that the only purpose of the government is to secure a representative body that can be entrusted with the expenditure of whatever money there may be in connection with the national celebration of the diamond jubilee of confederation in a manner that will be likely to accord with the desires and wishes of the people of Canada as a whole.

I mean industrial labour. I represent agriculture. Mr. Chairman, when the
committee rose at six o'clock it was considering a bill to incorporate a national committee for the celebration of the diamond jubilee of confederation, to cost 1250,000. I fail to see that there is any demand from the people of Canada for a celebration of the sixtieth anniversary of confederation. Why
should we spend $250,000 of the taxpayers' money for such a celebration when several hundred thousands of our citizens over in the United States will celebrate the anniversary of the Declaration of Independence on the fourth of July? Probably the Liberal party feel the need of celebrating their great victory of last September. We on this side of the House have not much to celebrate, but we hope to have in the years to come. We are not a practical people.
We cannot solve our most common economic problems. Talk about spending $250,000 on a diamond jubilee celebration! Mr. Chairman, let me tell you that there are over 160,000 returned men in the United States to-day who fought for their country on the battlefields of France and Flanders-a country that they have had to get out of. More than 50.000 of those gallant men lie buried where they fell fighting for France. Six thousand men from Toronto, many of them Orangemen, lie dead there. They fought for France and the French language, a land that expelled the Huguenots, and as I say, many of them were from Tory and Orange Toronto.
The only demand for this celebration is from a lot of Canadian clubs that are no more Canadian than Empire clubs are imperial. If this $250,000 is intended to celebrate the brilliant dream of empire under the principle of separatism, to emphasize our new status, all very well and good, let the Prime Minister put it in the preamble of the bill. But why celebrate the sixtieth anniversary of confederation? Confederation has not been such a shining success that we should desire to spend $250,000 on its celebration. With the economic problems now confronting this country I see no occasion to shout from the housetops about our status and our diamond jubilee.
I hold in my hand, Mr. Chairman, a book containing an attack on Sir John Macdonald, one of the pillars and founders of confederation, written by W. Stewart Wallace, librarian of the university of Toronto. This is the kind of textbook that is used in the university of Toronto, a textbook attacking the great founder of confederation. Perhaps to be fair to the professor I should read his actual words:
There are few figures in Canadian history on whom the historian finds it more difficult to pass judgment than on Sir John Macdonald. In his lifetime he was either loved or execrated; and to this day opinion is divided with regard to him.
Those who contend that his was a pernicious influence in Canadian history are not without reasons for their belief. He had some grave faults. He was for many years addicted to
