the heavy drinking habits of his day and generation, and his behaviour was not always such as befitted the prime minister of a great dominion. He did very little to raise the moral tone of political life in Canada during his lifetime, or afterwards. He studied human nature, as Gold win Smith said, "perhaps too much on the weak side". If he was a past master in the management of men, it was by playing on their foibles and weaknesses, rather than by appealing to their better natures. Though himself above the acceptance of a bribe, he was not above the indirect bribery of other men. There was, indeed, in the rough-and-tumble of political warfare, hardly a weapon in his armoury which he would not use. The ' Pacific Scandal", the gerrymander of 1882, the Dominion Franchise Act of 1885-these are only illustrations of the lengths to which he was prepared to go.
That is a straight libel on the great founder of confederation, the man who made this country what it is to-day, the man who put protection on the statute books. And we are asked to pay $250,000 of the people's money on a celebration of the diamond jubilee of confederation when one of its principal founders is thus libelled by an employee of the Ontario government, a professor in the university of Toronto! If the Canadian clubs and the Empire clubs want to have such a celebration let them pay for it. As I say, we on this side have not much cause to indulge in a celebration. And I admit that our United Farmers of Ontario friends are pretty much in the same position in view of the two last general elections in the province of Ontario; they have nothing to celebrate. But if they do wish to celebrate, let them hold forth banners with such inscriptions as. " Platforms are to get in on, not to stand on." " Free trade for Canada." Free trade for Canada, Mr. Chairman, has driven hundred of thousands of our men to the United States where on the next fourth of July they will help celebrate the Declaration of Independence.
I am not a bigoted Conservative; I am a very moderate party man, because there is a lot of good on the other side of the House as well as here. Our friends opposite secured a majority at the last election, and we have to be good enough sports to congratulate them on their victory, we have to be good enough sports to admit that they are a pretty good looking body of men, from the young Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice -a handsome young man-to their humblest member. We admit over here that we have not much to celebrate. We put our party in the cemetery last September, and once you get in a cemetery, whether you are an individual or a political pairty, nothing but a miracle will get you out.

Here is another textbook which is put into the hands of the school children of the province. Let us see what it has to say:
After the election of 1887, Mr. Blake retired from the leadership of the Liberals, and then they chose a man destined to play a part in Canada second only to that of Macdonald. Perhaps the most striking characteristic of Wilfrid Laurier was his courtly manners. Politics in Canada had lacked the graces of life. Such terms as "trickster", "imbecile", "traitor", were too often heard; Macdonald himself once called an opponent in parliament a pup and threatened to "slap his chops." Laurier, however, bore himself with stately dignity. He was never off his guard, and liis sternest denunciations were always on a high level of refinement. Men were, indeed, tempted to think him a dreamy scholar, while, in fact, he could, as need arose, be stern and strong. It was something that, at a time when racial and religious feeling was acute over the Riel question, a French-Canadian and a Roman Catholic should be chosen as sole leader of the Liberal party. In earlier days a French leader like Cartier had had to share authority with an English-speaking colleague; but national unity in Canada had grown, and now, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, the Liberals followed Laurier and in the end carried him into power.
I have nothing whatever to say against the Liberal party. They will be welcomed in Toronto at any time, and I may tell hon. gentlemen that that city has no bigotry. Sir Wilfrid Laurier was popular in Ontario among the Conservatives as well as the Liberals and he gave the country what he thought was good government. But it will be seen from this quotation what sort of literature is put into the hands of the school children.
Now, I fail to see what we have to celebrate. We are not practical people. Here we are proposing to celebrate confederation and the government apparently fails to consider the situation of the returned men. What room is there for rejoicing when you think of the position of these men and when you reflect upon the hundreds of thousands of our Canadians who have been driven across the border into the United States to look for jobs as a result of the free trade policy of the government? About the only people who are getting any really good jobs are the members of the committee of ambassadors which this government has appointed, ambassadors to all the countries in the seven seas, one of whom has just gone to Washington. I say, there is nothing for us to celebrate, and the Canadian people are not given to that sort of thing. The only occasion on which you can get a decent parade in Toronto is the twelfth of July, not the first. Then you can muster from twelve to fifteen thousand people in the parade. Strange as it may seem, many of those who view the great

Diamond Jubilee oj Confederation
walkout and attend the picnic at Exhibition park are Catholics. But apart from that, parades generally are a flat failure. And in any case the first of July is not by any means an ideal time for any great demonstration. The weather is too hot.
I have nothing to say against the men and women who are selected for this committee. But there are thousands of our citizens in the United States who will look with mixed feelings upon this celebration. It seems to me that we ought to make some attempt to settle our economic problems with a view to preventing the further exodus of Canadians to the United States, and let those who want to celebrate pay for it. The money could be spent to far better purpose in giving employment to needy men generally, and particularly to our returned soldiers. Many of our returned men sacrificed all they had in the interests of the country and now they are getting a raw deal. The Canadian clubs which are behind this movement are no more Canadian than the imperial clubs are imperial. This $250,000 will be spent on a few banquets, the playing of a few party tunes, and generally the raising of a great hullaballoo, and everybody will be saying what a huge success confederation has been. That is all very well; but has confederation been such a success when you come to think of it? Does the Duncan report lead us to think so? Are all these various problems which are pressing for a solution likely to be settled in such a way as they would be if confederation were so successful as to warrant the celebration contemplated? I know a lot of people who will celebrate the confederation of Canada. They are the American millionaires who have come over here and seized our waterpowers to exploit the products of our forests, mines, and other resources. Canada is the happy hunting ground of such people and these American millionaires will certainly shout loud hurrahs, for they have reason to do so. I do not blame the Dominion government for having given away the resources of the country which we Canadians ought to develop for ourselves. The provincial premiers are in many instances to blame. In Ontario, at any rate, various premiers have surrendered to the American millionaires more territory than was given away to favoured people in the time of George III.
I have said before, and I repeat it on this occasion; what this country needs is a Mussolini who will stand up firmly for the rights of the people and protect our interests in various directions, in lumbering, fishing, mining, agriculture and so forth against encroachment from outside. What has Mussolini done for
his country? Let me quote one very significant statement of his: "We have translated into action what we promised in words." Have we ever heard of any prime minister here translating into action what he promised in words? Mussolini says:
A recent example of how the spirit of silent work has thoroughly saturated our people is shown in the construction of the new railroad along the Ionian sea in Calabra. The work of constructing this railroad has gone on silently and laboriously for many months. Thirteen new and extensive bridges have been built, and yet not in a single case was there a speech delivered, whereas formerly such events were accompanied by orations and the blare of trumpets, the clapping of hands and great shouts of joy. The joy was there and the events popular, but no speeches overdid it with useless words.

Mr. Speaker, I
rise to a point of order. Just what bearing has this discussion?

They don't celebrate in
Italy. They do things. I am referring to the way they do things in Italy. Even if there were a constituency of Long Lake there, they would not spend money in it for a celebration like this. Actions speak louder than words.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I was just going to ask my friend to address his remarks a little more closely to the matter before the committee.

I think I am quite in
order, Mr. Chairman, and if necessary I can cite the authorities. When we come to that particular section I would like to make a motion that the amount to be spent be reduced to $1,000, because the people are opposed to such extravagance by the government. We are spending $250,000 on a celebration when we have nothing to celebrate. Are we to celebrate the exodus or our new status, this new dream of empire under which we are a separate country and can make our own treaties, under which we have an ambassador going down to Washington? Are we to spend $250,000 of the taxpayers' money to celebrate our becoming the Mexico of the north?
I could go on almost indefinitely, but I would suggest to the Prime Minister that during the celebration a portrait of the board of strategy, accompanied by a portrait of the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) should be unveiled and would probably be suitable for presentation to the museum. I might also suggest that a portrait of Sir Henry Thornton, who, according to the subsidized press of this country, was the real discoverer of this country instead of Christopher Columbus, should be unveiled at the same time. With the rate of
416	COMMONS
Diamond Jubilee of Confederation
taxation in Canada going up by leaps and bounds, with the income tax and sales tax as high as they are, we should postpone the celebration until such time as we can solve our own problems and prevent this country from becoming the happy hunting ground of a lot of American millionaires who are picking up timber limits, water power, mines and pulpwood areas, and in doing so driving hundreds of thousands of men from Canada to another country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
At six o'clock
1	mentioned to the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) that if she and the hon. members who sit around her would give me the names of two or three representative personages to be added to the committee I would be pleased to do so provided they were of a character which would make the committee more acceptable to all parties in the House. The names handed me were those of Mr. Tom Moore, President of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada; Mr. M. J. Cold-well, President of the Canadian Teachers' Association; Mr. Henry Wise Wood, President of the United Farmers of Alberta and Mr. Michael Luchkovich, one of the hon. members of this House. I might say that Mr. Luchkovich is one of the first members to come into the House representing a large number of citizens from foreign lands who have become naturalized Canadians, and it was thought that his name on the committee would appeal to many of our naturalized citizens. To those names I would suggest that we add the names of Mr. George F. Edwards, President of the Canadian Council of Agriculture and Hon. Cyrille F. Delage, President of the Council of Public Instruction of the province of Quebec. Those names will make the committee more representative and I hope hon. members will feel that with these additions the committee will be sufficiently representative to commend itself to the House generally. I therefore beg to make the following motion:
That the following words be inserted in clause
2	after the word "Canada" in the fortieth line of page 2 of the bill:
Tom Moore, Esquire, President of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada;
Michael Luchkovich, Esquire, M.P.
Mr. J. Coldwell, Esquire, President of the Canadian Teachers' Federation.
Hon. Cyrille F. Delage, President of the Council of Public Instruction of the province of Quebec.
Henry Wise Wood, Esquire, President of the United Farmers of Alberta.
George F. Edwards, Esquire, President of the Canadian Council of Agriculture.

I have not the least objection to the motion nor have I any objection to the names mentioned, but I do think the Prime Minister has demeaned himself and his position after the statement he made before six o'clock, when he said that it was not his intention to have on this committee the representative of any class; now he comes into the House and moves for such representation. I might point out to him, if I so desired, that on this list there are no names representing the men who served overseas. I am not suggesting that such names should be added; I think the Prime Minister was right in his contention that this should be a committee representative of Canadians, not of class, and I much deprecate the change in 'his attitude.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As far as demeaning myself is concerned, I may say to the hon. member who has just spoken that I am quite prepared to do that again if I can help to bring about unanimity in this House in a matter that seems simple justice. Hon. members looking over the names originally presented will recognize the fact that the two old political parties, so-called, are very largely and in fact almost exclusively represented therein. In this House are others belonging to a group representing a considerable portion of this country, and from that group I have received certain of these names not as representatives of class but as the representatives of many of those of our fellow citizens who, in the opinion of that particular group, will thereby be given an added interest in the work of the committee. With regard to the returned soldiers, I think if the hon. member will read over the names he would find among them that of Lieutenant General Sir Percy Lake, K.C.B., K.C.M.G., President of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League. This organization, I understand, embraces the various returned soldiers' organizations and it is in that representative capacity that the name of Sir Percy Lake has been inserted. There are also the names of Major General Mewburn, and one or two others who will be quickly recognized as representative of the men who served overseas. In addition my hon. friend will find among those who are named a very considerable number who were quite as active in the war as we all know he himself was. I think, therefore, the interests of all have been carefully taken care of.

These appointees were
asked for as class representatives. That is what I object to.
4X7

Diamond Jubilee oj Confederation

May I voice my appreciation of the kindness of the Prime Minister? When I said, possibly quite shortly, this afternoon that 1 did not know who had used my name without asking my consent, I may have appeared somewhat unkind but I had no such intention. However, so much was said in the budget as to the whole prosperity of Canada depending upon agriculture and industry that one could not help thinking that a committee to be representative of the whole Dominion must include some of these people. I appreciate very much what has been done, which I think is only fair, and if we use this opportunity to help other people in other parts of the world to understand Canada and at the same time use this movement to arouse in Canadians a pride in their own country and a national spirit-a spirit that will help us to go on and meet the troubles or the problems of the future-we surely can do much for our country. I hope that as one of the committee I may be of some slight assistance.

Motion agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
On section 3-Objects.

May I point out to the
Prime Minister that among the objects of the corporation is the administration and distribution of the grant mentioned and any further grant or grants hereafter made. Clause 14 provides that a sum not exceeding $250,000 is to be paid towards defraying the expenses of the corporation. Does the reference to grants hereafter made contemplate grants to be made by this parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The last clause to which my hon. friend referred indicates the amount that parliament is appropriating by this bill. It is possible that at some future date parliament may appropriate an additional amount.
It will be parliament that will do that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. As far
as public moneys are concerned, no addition will be made to the amount named except with the consent of parliament.

Even should parliament not be sitting when the requisition is made? Supposing parliament has adjourned and the committee believes it requires more money-it may not really need the money but believes it does-will there be an order in council authorizing an additional expenditure?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The committee will be given to understand that the wish of parliament is that it should keep the expenditure within the amount appropriated. If the committee when it meets finds that the amount is not going to be sufficient it will be its duty so to advise parliament at a very early date.
Section 4 agreed to.
On section 5-Executive committee.

It does not seem
quite advisable that the expenditure of $250,000 should be left to an executive committee of six persons, yet that is what we are doing. This number out of a membership of sixty-nine can go ahead, make the necessary arrangements, and expend this money. Such a quorum seems unusually small out of a total membership of sixty-nine. Seeing that quite a number of members are within easy reach of the capital, it seems only reasonable that the quorum of six should be larger.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I point out to my hon. friend that the clause to which he refers reads:
Until otherwise provided by by-law or regulation made by the executive committee, six members of the executive committee shall be a quorum.
If, when this large body assembles, it has any reason to feel that this particular clause does not provide the necessary number it can pass a by-law immediately requiring a larger number to be present when certain expenditures are being authorized. The Canadian patriotic fund, as I recall it, ran into an expenditure of millions of dollars. The original committee was a large one, but it was found necessary to have a small executive to administer the fund. I think the language here is taken from the act that, established the Canadian patriotic fund. I think my hon. friend will find that is the way most large corporations find it advisable to transact their business.
I was not objecting to the size of the executive committee. I was pointing out the possibility of a small number being entrusted with the carrying out of very important work.

This is a very large committee, and a great many of the members live at a long distance from this city. Is it contemplated that the expenses of this committee should come out of the fund? Because if you take the expenses of nearly a



Diamond Jubilee oj Confederation
hundred people the amount is going to run into a lot of money. We are not going to be through with the expense when we spend $250,000. That is evident. Is it worth the money? For my part I do not think it is.

In view of the fact that a number of names were mentioned to-night 'as well as the other evening of persons whom it would be desirable to have on the committee, would it not be wise to provide that the executive committee should have power to add to their number?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: So they have.

The members
of various associations might be omitted although it might be important that their names should be added. I see no provision in clause 5 or clause 6 for making that addition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is some such provision in the bill.

There is nothing to prevent any six members of the committee constituting themselves an executive and no provision in case they fail to attend meetings for notifying others. It would be quite possible for the Prime Minister to have a coterie of his own in such a case as that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I can assure
my hon. friend that the Prime Minister has no intention of doing anything of the kind. I confess I am rather surprised that he should make that 'particular remark. If he has any amendment he wishes to move to this clause, I am sure the committee would be pleased to receive it.

I do not want to move an
amendment. I simply want all the members of the committee to be. notified, and not only six.

There is a little defect
in this clause and I think the point is well taken. Subclause 2 reads:
The persons whose names are mentioned in section 2 shall constitute the provisional executive committee, and provided that six of the said persons are present at the meetings, the corporation may be organized and the executive committee may be elected by them.
There is no provision for the calling of the meetings. If six members of the committee saw fit to meet at Ottawa, I do not know who could take objection to their doing so. There is no provision in this clause for notice. A meeting of the committee should be called and provision should be made for notice. Then if some members do not attend, let six do the work.
[Mr. Chaplin.!

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend must realize that any notice sent out for the calling of a meeting of the committee would be sent to every member of the committee in plenty of time for every member to be present. One of the officers of state will be charged with the duty of notifying all the members to come to Ottawa on a particular date. The press of the country will have ample notice of the particular date on which they will be assembled. If there was the slightest danger of members not being notified, I would say; Certainly add more clauses to the bill. May I draw my hon. friend's attention to this point? The government of which he was a member drew up a bill to administer the Canadian patriotic fund. This bill, as I mentioned to the House the other day, is modelled on that bill, clause for clause. I so directed when the bill was being drafted. I do not think anyone would have presumed that the Prime Minister of that day was seeking to gather a few favourites around him to administer the Canadian patriotic fund. Surely we can discuss these things with each other as gentlemen.

I quite agree with that,
but the bill goes into some formal matters and this is a simple question that could be settled now by way of amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Move the
amendment.

Just insert the words:
The persons whose names are mentioned in section 2 shall be duly called together for the first meeting of the said committee.
And state that six are a quorum as provided in the bill. Supposing they were not called together, supposing half a dozen were omitted in the notice and they felt offended or affronted or legal action resulted, that would be very unpleasant. I am only suggesting a difficulty might arise. I am quite willing to take the word of the Prime Minister that no difficulty will arise, but it is quite easy to have provision made for notice of the first meeting.
As there is no provision for notice, can not it be taken for granted that the first names on the committee will be the conveners?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
First of all,
might I answer the leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie)? Without knowing what amendment he will propose, I will say in advance that I shall be pleased to accept it. This is not a party measure in any way, and

Diamond Jubilee oj Confederation
I am anxious to meet the wishes of the committee as a whole. If my hon. friend (Mr. Brown) wishes to insert the name of any individual to call the committee, I am sure it would also be a pleasure to insert it. The same method of calling together this committee will be adopted as was adopted in calling together the Canadian patriotic fund committee.
What was that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I understand
the Under-Secretary of State or some permanent official of the government sent communications to all the parties whose names were mentioned, asking them to meet at Ottawa on a particular date. I do not think it will strengthen the matter to name any particular, official to call the committee, but if that is the desire of hon. members, we shall have that inserted.
Is it the purpose to have a series of celebrations or simply to have one big celebration at Ottawa?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The government has no desire to dictate what form this celebration shall take, whether it shall be one celehration at Ottawa, whether it shall be celebrations in the different provinces, whether it shall be along educational lines or along the lines of display in one form or another. The purpose of calling the committee is to let the committee decide all that. Once the committee is chosen, it will be the body that makes that decision.

If there is to be one
celehration in the capital city, probably the amount that is being appropriated will be sufficient; but if, as one of my hon, friends has suggested, there is going to be a series of celebrations, one in each provincial capital for example, then the amount that is being appropriated will not be sufficient. That must be clear to any person. I presume before this parliament prorogues, we shall have some idea as to the scope of the general celebrations from one end of the country to the other. Is that the expectation of the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If this debate does not continue too long, it is.

I am just trying to get
this thing right because I am strongly in favour of this celebration. The sixtieth anniversary of our birth as a nation is a great event in Canada, and it should be celebrated with all proper dignity and enthusiasm. My idea would be that this committee might go even further- than have a series of celebrations in the different provinces, and might encourage local celebrations wherever they can be organized so as to make the day one of general observance from coast to coast. That would be my idea of a great observance of the sixtieth anniversary qf our confederation. I want to see enough money appropriated to carry out the thing properly, and I would suggest to the Prime Minister that before the House rises, some effort should be made to ascertain from any executive committee that may be formed the extent of their plan so that sufficient money may be provided to carry it out in a proper and dignified fashion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I can assure my hon, friend that is in all probability exactly what the executive committee will do, namely, to announce at as early a date as possible the plans proposed, and I hope that will be done before parliament rises.

Has there been any communication from the provincical governments as to whether they will assist in the financial undertaking? I quite agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Hocken) that the amount appropriated in this bill is absolutely inadequate. If the sixtieth anniversary of the birth of the Canadian nation, as we are now called, is going to be fittingly celebrated, it seems to me we shall need many times that amount of money. We all know that as a general rule the government or party that will lead in expenditure will be allowed to do the paying. It would be right and proper that the provincial governments should be first sounded out to discover what contributions they will make.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The expectation I should think would be that the provinces would wish to have provincial celebrations and to make appropriations therefor. Once this committee is formed, one of its functions will be to get immediately into touch with the provinces in order to ascertain what they are prepared to do.

Will the committee
work in conjunction with the provinces or separately?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is in the bill a clause which indicates that one of the purposes is to coordinate the work between the provinces and the Dominion.

The remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. McGibbon) are of course his personal opinion and 'he is welcome to it. In my opinion this sum is ample; it is indeed too much. I wish to register a protest against any effort on the part of any hon. member to increase the amount to 'be voted. If any provinces are
420	COMMONS
Diamond Jubilee of Confederation
so very anxious to enter into a celebration at the same time, let it vote its own money. I think an appropriation of $250,000 or a quarter of a million for a celebration, when, as the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) said, there were so many soldiers and others out of work, anxious to get jobs and earn something, is extraordinary and ridiculous.

We heard a story this
afternoon of a bounding prosperity. There is nobody out of work.

To which
the hon. member's party did not agree.

We have heard this afternoon that prosperity in this country is so great that everybody is at work. I think, Mr. Chairman, that the particular responsibility for this celebration rests upon this parliament. This is the parliament of confederation. It represents every province in Canada, and why should not the national treasury stand the whole cost of a proper celebration of that day, giving proper consideration to each province that desires to take part in it? I do not know; I may be a different kind of Canadian from my hon. friend from Bow River.
Hear, hear.
I was born here, and I am a real Canadian. I am not one of the imported variety, and perhaps I have a different feeling towards this Dominion than my hon. friend has.

I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I too am a real Canadian, a real Canadian for three or four generations, and I protest against language of that kind being used against any member duly elected to this House.

As usual, my hon. friend from Winnipeg messes in where he has no right to get, and raises a point of order that is not a point of order at all. If there is any man in the House to *whose speeches objections can be made upon this ground, it is my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre. I am urging, Mr. Chairman, for a dignified and suitable celebration of our natal day. I do that. as a Canadian born, and if there are any people in this country who are imported Canadians and who do not see the thing as I do, of course, they are entitled to their own opinion, but I have a seat in this House and I stand for Canada and Canadians, and I want Canadians on this occasion to show the world that they are capable of appreciating the [Mr. E. J. Garland.1
wonderful heritage they have and the privileges they enjoy, and mark in a befitting manner the progress we have made in this country in the past six decades. We could go further than that, and in this celebration not only draw attention to our past accomplishments, but do a great deal perhaps to inspire the young men of this country to a greater love and a higher respect for their own nation, and if that is part of the result it will be money well spent no matter how much it costs.

The amendment which I propose, Mr. Chairman, and which may get us over a difficulty in the future, reads as follows:
That subsection 2 of section 5 be amended by inserting after the word "committee' in line 24 the following words:
The said committee shall hold its first meeting at the city of Ottawa. The Secretary of State for Canada shall convene the first meeting of said committee by notice in writing sent by post to the members thereof.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 6-Co-operation with other bodies.

I am not clear as to just what is meant by a celebration. It is not the intention, I take it, to permit all this money to be expended upon a demonstration. I understand that the committee will be permitted to expend money in any direction they see fit in order to bring home to the people the significance of this great event. The anniversary of the confederation of Canada is one of the outstanding events in our whole history, and from the time it was first mentioned in the speech from the throne, I have endeavoured to induce my own constituency to centre upon this historic event. I think that is giving a proper lead to the people. As to the expenditure of money, I have asked our county council to do one or two things. I have asked them to gather together photographs of the men who sat in this first parliament and passed the confederation act. This they are undertaking to do at their own expense, and in other ways they are preparing to mark this great event. Am I right in my impression that some of the money under the control of the committee will be used in directing affairs of that kind? Would that come within the scope of the .committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think my
hon. friend is entirely right, and that what he has just described would come within the

Diamond Jubilee of Confederation
scope of the committee's activities. TheTe have been a great many proposals made as to how the diamond jubilee should be commemorated; I will use that word instead of " celebrated," as it perhaps will explain away the idea of a mere spectacle. Some of these suggestions have related to educational aspects, others to pageants and the like. There have been no end of suggestions come to the government in one form and another from persons throughout the country as to what would be the most appropriate thing to do. The government intends to hand over to this committee every suggestion that has .been submitted, and allow the committee to adopt or reject as it sees fit, in other words to draw up a program of its own.
I might make mention of another feature. The government is being asked to contribute advertisements to publications with respect to Canada in the sixtieth year of confederation. We have felt that unless some committee is placed in charge of that work, there will be no control of expenditure on such advertising and publicity, and our purpose is to turn over to this committee that phase also of the celebration.

Section agreed to.
Sections 7 to 10 inclusive agreed to.
On section 11-Head office.

Inasmuch as the committee seems to be open to suggestions, it might be well to put on record this idea. Throughout the Dominion a great many community affairs, some political, some non-political, are held on the first of July, and the theme of the addresses on this particular day might well centre around this great event that we are commemorating. I think the suggestion might well be passed on to the committee that each of these constituencies be given SI ,000 of this $250,000 fund in order that they may celebrate in a proper manner the sixtieth birthday of confederation and so arouse the whole country to a realization of the significance of this great event in our national life.

Section agreed to.
Section 12 agreed to.
On section 13-July 2 a public holiday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I might explain to the House that as July 1 this year comes on Friday the government thought it would be the wish of parliament to have Saturday declared a public holiday as well. There would thus be three consecutive holidays for the celebration.

Does this mean
that July 1 will also be a public holiday?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, July 1 is a statutory holiday.

Section agreed to.
On section 14-$250,000 granted to the corporation.

Mr. Chairman, the
Prime Minister has intimated that once this corporation meets it may approach the government and parliament for further sums of money. Whether parliament will be able to control the granting of such further sums will depend on its being in session. Therefore I would ask the Prime Minister to give an undertaking to this House that no further sums of money will be granted for the celebration unless passed by parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I hesitate to give an undertaking in those specific words. I will inform the executive committee of what I have said in the House; indeed my first duty will be to give to the committee a copy of the debate which has taken place on this very subject. But I am unable to say what may take place after this parliament adjourns and before it meets again. Conceivably some expenditure might have to be made in the interim, for example, in connection with the visit of His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales and the Prime Minister of Great Britain. A certain amount might be required in addition to what is here proposed which could not be foreseen and which it would be essential to grant. I should not like to bind the government in such a manner that we would1 not be able to carry out the celebration on a scale befitting the occasion. In saying that, however, let me state to my hon. friend that the executive committee will be advised of what I gather to be the view of this parliament, that they should seek to confine their expenditure to the amount here set forth. If the expenditure runs beyond the $250,000, there will have to be good and sufficient reasons furnished-reasons that at least in the opinion of the government would meet with the approval of parliament.

Mr. Chairman, while I am
not altogether opposed to this bill, I do think that $250,000 is an ample amount for the city of Ottawa to celebrate our diamond jubilee, seeing that other places will have to stand their own expenditure for this purpose.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Let me correct my hon. friend. This is not an expenditure for the city of Ottawa alone. This fund will

Montreal Harbour Commission
be handled by a national committee. It is to cover the expense of what that committee may decide to do from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Undoubtedly certain features of the celebration will take place in Ottawa, but it may be assumed that a large proportion of this money will go to meet expenses incidental to much that will be done outside the capital.

I think $250,000 should be
the limit, and therefore I propose the following amendment to section 14:
That after the word "Act" the following words be added, "and that it shall be understood that no further grant from this parliament shall be made".

Mr. Chairman, I hope
the Prime Minister will not accept the amendment. This celebration should be held in a manner in keeping with the dignity of the nation, and to tie the hands of the committee to an expenditure that is after all only an average of $1,000 for each riding in the whole Dominion is to my mind cutting the expenditure down very low indeed. I hope the Prime Minister and his government if they are going to proceed with this celebration will not so tie the hands of the committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the government cannot suppport the amendment of my hon. friend, and I hope the committee will not accept it.
Amendment negatived.

speechtext:
Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill No. 60, to provide for a loan to the harbour commissioners of Montreal.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 2-Loan of $12,000,000 to the corporation.

maintopic: MONTREAL HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $12,000,000 FOE TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I purposely refrained from saying anything on the second reading of the bill, because I did not wish it to appear that I intended delaying the minister. There is however a very serious question which I wish to direct to the attention of the committee and to have discussed at this point. It is rather difficult for one to determine precisely the right moment to bring this matter up,

but I am inclined to think it should be done on this section. I refer to the absence from this bill of a section which appears in acts of a similar character and which in the present measure should be numbered 6, providing for the repayment of the loan. The minister may have a complete and satisfactory explanation to offer, but I think the committee ought to be made aware of all the facts before proceeding with the bill. What may be described as the original act in legislation of this character was passed in the year 1896, and similar bills went through this House in 1922 and*1923. In 1922 a bill almost identical in terms with the present one was adopted, the only difference being that it contained the following:
The principal and interest of the sums advanced to the corporation under the authority of this act shall be paid by the corporation out of its revenue mentioned in section 8 of chapter 10 of the Statutes of 1896 (first session) and shall be charged upon the said revenue in the same manner and to the same extent as if the sum so advanced had been borrowed by the corporation under the said chapter 10.
In 1923 a similar bill was passed for the same purpose of advancing moneys to the Montreal harbour board and a similar section was incorporated in it. I shall read precisely the provision made in that case; it varies slightly from the first:
The principal and interest of the sums advanced to the corporation under the authority of this act shall be paid by the corporation out of all its property and assets, and out of all its tolls, rates, dues, penalties and other sources of revenue and income whatsoever, and shall rank as a charge thereon, and have precedence in regard to payment next after the- payments provided for in section 8, of chapter 10 of the Statutes of 1896.
In the statute of 1896 the section 8 referred to in these two acts provides:
The principal and interest of the sums of money which may be borrowed .... shall be paid out of the revenue arising from the rates and penalties-
And so forth. Then it sets forth the standing of 'the various charges against such revenues:
(a)	Payment of all expenses incurred in the collection of the said revenue, and other indispensable charges;
(b)	The defraying of the expenses attendant on keeping the harbour clean, and on keeping the wharfs and other works therein in a thorough state of repair;
(e) The payment of interest due on all sums of money borrowed under this act or under any of the acts repealed by The Montreal Harbour Commissioners Act, 1894, without priority or preference;
(d) The paying off of the principal of such sums.

Montreal Harbour Commission
I want the committee to note that in the original bill provision is made for the repayment of principal and interest out of the earnings of the harbour. In the two acts to which I have referred, passed in 1922 and 1923, measures similar in every respect to this bill, provision is made for precisely the same thing, mention of which is made in the section of the act of 1896 to which I have alluded, namely, that the principal and interest shall be repaid out of the earnings of 'the harbour, out of dues, collections and so forth.
Last year, when this bill was first brought to the attention of parliament, a notice of motion was given by the minister. That notice of motion, given on June 7, 1926, provided :
That it is expedient to authorize a loan to the harbour commissioners of Montreal in an amount not exceeding $12,000,000 to carry on the construction of terminal facilities, upon approval by the governor in council of detailed plans, specifications and estimates for such works and the deposit of debentures of the corporation to cover said loan

The committee would do well to note this particularly:
-and further, to establish a sinking fund to be applied to the reduction of the debenture indebtedness of the corporation to His Majesty.
On June 9, two days afterwards, when the resolution of which notice had been given appeared on the order paper, these significant words to which I have just referred were found to have been omitted. In the first place the resolution ought not to have been changed; it ought, not to have appeared on the order paper except in the form of which notice had been given. The words to which I have referred, namely :
And further, the establishment of a sinking fund to be applied to the reduction of the debenture indebtedness of the corporation to His Majesty-
-were omitted from the resolution appearing on the order paper of June 9, 1926.
After this somewhat lengthy preamble I come to the bill now before the House. In every particular it follows the acts of 1922 and 1923 with the one exception that section 6 is left out. I have already intimated that this section 6 is the clause under which provision is made for the repayment of the sums advanced. Let me read from the bill of 1923, in order to remind the committee of what has been dropped:
The principal and interest of the sums advanced to the corporation under the authority of this act shall be paid by the corporation out of all its property and assets, and out of all its tolls, rates, dues, penalties and other sources
of revenue and income whatsoever, and shall rank as a charge thereon, and have precedence in regard to payment next after the payments provided for in section 8 of chapter 10 of the Statutes of 1896, first session.
I submit in the first place that the minister should make a very clear explanation of the rather strange disappearance of this important clause; and I wish to emphasize that in connection with the harbour board of Montreal, which I have had reason both to compliment and to criticise in this House, that corporation has provided for the repayment of these loans out of its earnings and has carefully prej served the practice of paying the interest. It has done that because of these sections to which I have referred, which make it obligatory upon the harbour commissioners to provide out of their earnings for repayment of both principal and interest. I am going to listen to what the minister has to say in explanation, and unless he can give me complete assurance that the practice so well established is to be followed in this case, I will later move for the addition of this clause. It is passing strange, however, that this clause, which has appeared in all the other acts to which I have referred, is now dropped. I made inquiry from the law officers of this House as to why this bill was different from the preceding bills, because the minister himself told us the other day that this bill was the same as that passed last year, and was similar to those passed on previous occasions. I was rather inclined to accept the bill as merely a routine measure, the main question being whether we should grant the $12,000,000, but as a matter of fact it is very much different from the others.

placed in my hands by the officers of the department a sinking fund of one and one-half per cent was provided for and I thought that most unfair. Montreal Harbour Commission

speechtext:
I hesitate to delay the committee, but the minister is surely not serious in the suggestion that if an hon. member rises in his place and says: I would like to have an audit of the port of Montreal, the minister would immediately grant it. Why, on the very face of it-I hesitate to use the word, but it is absurd. charges as he desires to make, and we will then have them investigated. You would have to have some charge. I will give the minister and the committee two or three very cogent reasons why I think this should be done, and I shall not, in doing so, refer to the port of Montreal, for the simple reason that the minister persists in returning every argument as if it were particularly directed against the port of Montreal. I just as steadily persist that that is not my objective. It is the general principle I am fighting for, and that I fought for last year and the other night. This House from time to time grants sums running into the millions. To-night it is $12,000,000-I think this has been preceded by some $40,000,000 to this particular port, and Vancouver I believe has received some $15,000,000 or more-by way of loan on the debentures of these ports for general investment, and this House and the members of this House have no more right to scrutinize the expenditure of these moneys than has any person outside the House. Now that is wrong in principle. You ask me to give some reason. I will give you a oouple of good reasons.
This House granted the harbour commissioners of Vancouver a loan of $5,000,000, similar to this, for the purpose of improving that harbour. Now I am going to tell the House how a couple of million dollars of that loan was expended. In one instance the harbour commissioners bought a piece of land from a certain company controlled by a gentleman by the name of Mr. Gale, who, by the way, was a political candidate-I am just stating the facts-for the purpose of
42,S

Montreal Harbour Commission
constellating a jetty to carry grain carriers out for the delivery of grain to be loaded on ships. That jetty was constructed for the purpose of serving an elevator owned by a company owned by Mr. Gale and his associates. On that jetty, out of the moneys granted by this parliament, was spent the sum of approximately $1,000,000. The fixed charges, interest and sinking fund, against that amounted to $112,000 a year; I am now quoting from returns that have been laid on the table of the House. In the first year of its construction the harbour commissioners secured a revenue of $12,000, and laid out in fixed charges $112,000. The next year they got a revenue of I think $23,000 or $27,000, and they paid out $112,000 in fixed charges. The point there is this; In the first place, the harbour commissioners should never have made the expenditure. In the second place the money was spent extravagantly; the construction was very extravagant, and there has been no control over that expenditure except by auditors appointed by the commissioners themselves.
I will give another illustration. The harbour commissioners in Vancouver, out of one of these votes supplied them by the House, bought an elevator known as the Woodward elevator. A gentleman by the name of Woodward went to Vancouver some years ago, about 1921, and went into the elevator business. He went broke in the undertaking; he did not have sufficient capital, and he went to the commissioners and asked them to take it over. I heard that they had done so, as did the business people of Vancouver. I wrote a letter to the chairman of the harbour board and pointed out to him that if he took over that project it would probably cost him upwards of half a million dollars to put the institution in good shape, and that he would only lose money very heavily as a result. When he was in Ottawa attending the minister I warned the chairman again, and I warned the department against entering into that project. However, they went on. The commissioners bought the property, and it now stands a cost to the harbour commissioners of some $960,000 or $970,000. It is leased today, I think, at a rental of about $30,000 a year. An arithmetical calculation will show to what an extent this country has profited by that. What was the trouble? The expenditures were extravagantly made. Has there been any check on that expenditure? No. Why? Because this House has no control over it. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, an attempt was made a session or two ago to have these matters investigated, and what 
were we told? That we had no right to bring these accounts before the public account.3 committee for the simple reason that they were not under the Auditor General and did not come within that category. If we accept the minister's suggestion, or the suggestion of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, and leave these matters to be dealt with by the audit board, we members of the House have no means of investigating, none whatever. All that will happen is this: I can stand in my place and make charges and all that sort of thing, and then we get an audit board appointed. The audit board reports to the government, and there is no committee of this House investigating. The public accounts committee have no chance to investigate, nor has anyone connected with this parliament any right to investigate, no more right than any man outside the House.
What I have been trying to argue for the last three sessions-last session in particular I emphasized it, and previously in this session, and again I emphasize it now-is not that we should harrass these harbour boards. I am wholeheartedly behind the harbour boards of this country, such as are run in a proper manner, and I want to help them in every possible way. I will vote for this expenditure, but I do ask, as a matter of right to this House and as a matter of reasonable safeguard to the harbour commissioners themselves, that the Auditor General shall be placed in charge. These harbour boards appoint their own auditors. I submit now to any trained business man or accountant in this House, is it a sound thing to have the management of a concern appoint its own auditors? It is not sound; it is contrary to every business principle. I will admit that in many institutions the shareholders are indifferent to their rights and allow the management sometimes to nominate the auditors; but that is private business, and here we are dealing with public moneys. The principle which is sound in private and in public business is that tlie shareholders concerned-and this parliament represent the shareholders in this case-should appoint the auditors of the management, and not the management appoint the auditors to audit their own affairs. All we ask of the minister and of the government is that we, representing the people whose moneys are being expended, should have our auditor, the Auditor General, audit these accounts.
In regard to the suggestion made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, I wholly agree with him in this, that there are certain matters that must be kept private,

Montreal Harbour Commission
but there is not a sensible auditor in the country who does not know exactly what should be kept private and what should be made public. That is what they are trained for; that is their business, and there will be no difficulty whatever about that. I will assure the minister from my own knowledge of the auditing game, which has extended over a great many years, that I would never think of asking that secret, confidential information, or information that would harrass the board, be made public. But in the interest of the harbour boards themselves-and goodness knows they are harrassed enough politically and in other ways for advantages here and advantages there-in the interest of inspiring confidence in public affairs, and in the name of what is right ana fair, I ask on behalf of this House and the people of this country that the Auditor General should be put in charge of these harbour commissions, expending as they are millions of the people's money-$12,000,000 this year-and I hope the Vancouver harbour commissioners may later, perhaps not this session but next, get a further advance; and the same with other harbour commissioners. Montreal Harbour Commission
Every good Canadian admires the port and wants to build it up. But with all due respect to the minister, the time has come when the accounts of this port and all its contracts and other business transactions should, like those of the national railways, be placed before the public accounts committee of this parliament.
Although this government has contributed not a cent to the Toronto harbour commission, and although no charges were made against its administration, the minister ordered an inquiry, and the Central Liberal Association of Toronto asked the government to appoint a board of politicians to take charge of the inquiry, although the city council had appointed Sir Thomas White to conduct the proceedings. speechtext: Substantial reasons have been given why there should be a general application of the Audit Act to harbour commissions. maintopic: MONTREAL HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $12,000,000 FOE TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I think there is some misunderstanding regarding the relative positions of the various harbour commissions in Canada. It is not for the mere pleasure of appointing harbour commissions that these boards are established. They were established because it was felt at the time that the affairs of the ports could be better administered by that means than from the department in Ottawa through the ordinary officers of the government, and it was decided by those who first created the commissions -that it would be preferable to have reliable men of experience, familiar with the local conditions, dead with the affairs of the ports concerned, rather than leave their administration to the department. We must have confidence in the men we appoint, and if we are to drag the harbour commissioners before the public accounts committee every year and compel them to answer questions in detail with reference to the smallest transactions they superintend, it will be very hard indeed to find men of reputable standing who will be ready to undertake -the duties of harbour commissioners and expose themselves to all the criticism to which they might -be liable. This departure was made by previous governments and approved by this one because it was thought that the affairs of a port could be best administered in this manner. Of course, if we have no confidence in the commissioners, that is a different matter; but if we trust them sufficiently to appoint them to this responsible position we should be satisfied with the guarantees and the securities which are provided in the law as it stands.
These harbour commissions are becoming more general: witness -the Duncan report in its recommendation as to the advisability of having harbour commissions at Halifax and St. John. I maintain -that there exist already, in -the law as it stands, all the safeguards which we can reasonably require in a matter of this kind. I mentioned a moment ago one of the provisions of the Audit Act; there is another which is well worth considering. Sec-

Montreal Harbour Commission
tion 8 of the Audit Act provides that nothing contained therein shall impair the authority given by the Consolidated Revenue Act and Audit Act to the Auditor General of Canada. And if you refer to chapter 24 of the revised statutes of Canada, Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, section 63 you will find, with reference to the powers of the Auditor General, the following:
Besides the appropriation accounts of the grants of parliament, the Auditor General shall examine and audit, if required so to do by the Minister of Finance, and in accordance with any regulations which are prescribed for his guidance in that behalf by the Treasury board. . .
(g) any other public accounts which, though not relating directly to the receipts or expenditure of the Dominion of Canada, the Treasury board directs him to examine and audit.
So that section 63 of that act provides a safeguard, the Auditor General having power to audit "any other public accounts which, though not relating directly to the receipts or expenditure of the Dominion of Canada", and so forth. I contend that the harbour boards through the assistance which they are receiving come under subsection (g) of section 63 of chapter 24 of the act in question. "Any other public accounts" may be taken as including the accounts of harbour commissions, and I do not consider it fair to ask that all the affairs of the harbour boards in general should be submitted to the public accounts committee to be discussed in detail a year after the expenditure has been made. This is not going to prevent any expenditure; the public accounts committee does not deal with prospective expenditures but with 'those already made, and only by way of criticism can the government be checked if we are not as strict as some gentlemen think we should be. So even through the public accounts committee the safeguard would not be greater because the expenditures would be considered after they had been made. In view of the safeguards we already enjoy I think it only fair that the bill should go through in. its present form, which leaves matters in exactly the same position. The matter raised by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and supported by others is one which is worth consideration and I am ready to give it the best of my judgment. I will consult the Minister of Finance, by whom the Audit Act is administered, and if anything can properly be done to improve the control we may exercise over these boards, I am quite ready to do it provided we do not embarrass them or complicate their affairs.

On different occasions and in different parts of Canada I have heard criticisms of certain harbour boards, criticisms certainly not complimentary to those boards.
I am not saying anything against the Montreal harbour board or any other particular board, but I have received letters, some of which are on my files at present, charging some of these boards with taking part in politics and with using funds for political purposes which should be used for the harbours. I do not say that these statements are correct, although I have received them from most responsible citizens, but under the circumstances and while there is danger that these boards may be charged by some people at least with misconduct, would it not be in the interest of the boards themselves to have the Auditor General look into their accounts? It seems to me a most fair proposition. I am not charging any board with misconduct, but it certainly seems to me that the minister will be doing more justice even to the men who compose these boards, and these men should feel that they are receiving more justice, by having the Auditor General look through their accounts and clear them of the charges of misconduct which are being made rather freely in ordinary conversation throughout the country to-day. I believe the minister should promise to make it a general rule that all these harbour boards be put under the control, so far as expenditures are concerned, of the Auditor General.
Probably the minister has very good reasons for saying that it would not be fair to insist that these accounts be brought before the public accounts committee, and the members of the boards interlocuted lay >11 the members of that committee. We all know that outstanding men have taken positions on these boards; I can look back at members of the Montreal harbour board whom I have met in the past; they were outstanding men just as there are outstanding men on that board today. But I should think these men would also welcome this proposition, and I think the minister would be well advised in saying tonight that all these boards should have their accounts investigated by the Auditor General. If the boards have nothing of which to be ashamed, as the minister says he is confident they have not, they should welcome the investigation. I believe the minister should take the attitude that the Auditor General of Canada will investigate every one of these boards annually and report to this House.

maintopic: MONTREAL HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $12,000,000 FOE TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
In looking into this matter
I find that there are two acts, first the Board of Audit Act of 1925, and then the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, which is chapter 24 of the revised statutes. I find that in 1925 this parliament decided upon a certain policy with respect to the investigation of the accounts of certain public bodies such as the Canadian National Railway Company, the Canadian Government Merchant Marine Limited and other undertakings which are owned or carried on by the government of Canada, as well as any commission or other public body the operations [DOT] of which are carried on by appropriations from the treasury of Canada. This harbour commission therefore comes under the Board of Audit Act, section 4 of which provides:
It shall be the duty of the board to act in an advisory capacity to the Treasury Board and under its direction to inquire into and report with regard to any matters entrusted to it by the Treasury Board including the following:
Then it proceeds to provide for an inquiry into the accounts of the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Government Merchant Marine Limited and any harbour commission in Canada. This places it entirely within the discretion of the Treasury board as to whether any such public audit of the Montreal harbour commission or other commissions shall be made, and only when the Treasury board gives such direction is an audit of the accounts of such a commission made. It seems to me reasonable to suggest to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) who has charge of this bill, and also to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), that this Board of Audit Act might be so amended as to provide for annual audits of such commissions as the Montreal harbour commission, so as to not leave it entirely within the discretion of the Treasury board as to whether or not such audit should be 'hiade. If such annual audits are made, section 7 of the act applies, which sections says:
Each report of the board shall be laid before both houses of parliament within twenty-one days from the date of its receipt by the minister, or if parliament be not then in session, within the first twenty-one days of the session then next following.
I am inclined to agree with the minister that when such a report is laid before this House it is quite competent for any hon. member to move that it be referred for further consideration to the public accounts committee. If there is any doubt about it, however, the doubt might be set at rest by a further amendment, in case the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries should con-

sider such an amendment necessary. It might be clearly stated in clauses 6 and 7 that the report should be laid not only before the House but before the public accounts committee as well for its consideration. I can see no objection to that. Therefore we come back to the question as to whether the audit board is the proper authority to audit these accounts. I am subject to correction, but I do not understand that the Auditor General of Canada has anything to do with the accounts of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, or the accounts of the Canadian National Railways; I understand they have their own audit but come so far as public audit is concerned, under the Board of Audit Act of 1925? Is not that correct? I understand it to be so. Therefore I can see no reason why the harbour commission should be dealt with in any different way, in the matter of audit, from that in which the accounts of the (Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine- two corporations which are receiving and expending very large grants of public money- are dealt with. But I do see a reason why those reports should not-be made at the mere suggestion of the Minister of Finance. The report of the Board of Audit should be made annually; it should be compulsory for the board to 'make an annual investigation of the harbour commission's accounts and annually report upon them. Then the report should be placed before parliament, as now provided in section 7 of the act, and made available to the public accounts committee for further consideration. I can see no real objection- to following such a course as that. The contention is that these audits should be made by the Auditor General. I do not know that there is any virtue in an audit by that official which may not be found in an audit under the Board of Audit Act of 1925. I do not think that we should demand an explicit undertaking from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries tonight. But I think that he and the Minister of Finance should consider the whole matter and give it their careful attention, so that later on, when the estimates for the current year are under consideration, they might give us some assurance that either under the Board of Audit Act of 1925, or under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, which is chapter 24 of the revised statutes, an audit and report should be compulsory in each and every year, and that the report made as the result of such audit should not only be laid before parliament as now provided, but should go before the public accounts committee for such consideration as that body may deem necessary to give to it.

For instance, the question of fees enters into the matter. This is a board, we will say, not setting aside a sinking fund to take care of its principal investment. By statute and by regulation of the grain board under the Grain Act the private concern is kept down to the same fees that the public concern charges, but the private concern must take care of its principal and interest. So it is an unfair competition unless the harbour commissioners are compelled so to conduct their business that out of their revenues they shall take care of both principal and interest.
I submit therefore, in conclusion, that it is contrary to the original act of 1896, where it is specifically laid down that the principal and interest shall be taken care of, and which deals exactly with, first, the charges against making the loan; next keeping the harbour
and so on clean; and lastly, principal and interest. I submit to the minister that parliament should insist that these boards set up a sinking fund sufficient to take care of these loans as they mature.

maintopic: MONTREAL HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $12,000,000 FOE TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The last criticism of my
hon. friend is not well founded. There is no difference between this clause and the one which exists in the bill of 1896. The three last lines state "and shall be a charge upon the said revenue in the same manner and to the same extent as if tlhe sum so advanced had been borrowed by the corporation under the said chapter 10.'' So the loan is under the same restrictions as are provided in the bill of 1896.

maintopic: MONTREAL HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $12,000,000 FOE TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: My criticism was that the harbour commission is not carrying out the spirit of these statutes, and my criticism is based on the minister's own statement of a moment ago and his statement of some time ago. At some future time, when we have the estimates before us and can discuss the question generally without being constantly reminded that we are attacking the port of Montreal, I intend to discuss this question of providing sinking fund and the question of adequate protection in the way of audits.

Amendment agreed to.
Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
